nameStory: The Woodsorrel Mite gets its name from its favorite dining spot – the leaves of woodsorrel plants, those charming little shamrock-lookalikes that pop up in gardens and woodlands. These tiny mites have developed such a close relationship with woodsorrel that they're practically inseparable, like finding peanut butter with jelly. The scientific name 'harti' honors an early arachnologist who first described these minuscule plant-feeders.
description: The Woodsorrel Mite is an incredibly tiny spider mite that's barely visible to the naked eye, measuring less than half a millimeter across. These microscopic arachnids are pale yellowish-green to reddish in color, with oval-shaped bodies that look like tiny moving dots on plant leaves. Unlike true spiders, they don't build webs for catching prey – instead, they use their needle-like mouthparts to pierce plant cells and suck out the contents. You'll need a magnifying glass or hand lens to see any detail on these diminutive creatures.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely small, about the size of a grain of salt or smaller – you'll need magnification to see body details clearly

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Oval, soft-bodied appearance with no distinct separation between head and abdomen, feeling squishy if accidentally crushed

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Pale yellowish-green to brick-red coloration, often with two darker spots visible on the back when viewed under magnification

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Creates fine, silky webbing on woodsorrel leaves that feels sticky to the touch and causes yellow stippling damage to leaf surfaces

idTips.label: Habitat Association
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found on woodsorrel plants (Oxalis species), particularly the heart-shaped three-leaflet varieties

habitat: Look for Woodsorrel Mites on woodsorrel plants growing in partially shaded areas of gardens, woodland edges, and disturbed soils throughout New England. They prefer the common yellow woodsorrel that thrives in both wild areas and cultivated spaces, from sea level to moderate elevations. You'll most often find them on the undersides of the characteristic three-part leaves, especially in areas with consistent moisture.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as woodsorrel plants emerge, beginning to feed and reproduce on fresh young leaves. Look for the first signs of fine webbing on new growth.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with multiple overlapping generations creating visible webbing and stippled damage on woodsorrel leaves. Population numbers reach their highest during warm, dry weather.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues until first frost, with mites often concentrating on the last healthy woodsorrel leaves as plants begin to decline.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter in soil debris and leaf litter near host plants, becoming dormant until spring warmth returns.

funFact: Despite being nearly invisible to the naked eye, a single Woodsorrel Mite can lay up to 100 eggs in just three weeks, and under perfect conditions, can complete its entire life cycle from egg to adult in as little as 10 days – meaning you could theoretically have great-great-great-grandchildren mites all living together on the same leaf!
confusionNotes: Woodsorrel Mites are easily confused with other spider mites, but their exclusive association with woodsorrel plants is the key identifier – if it's not on woodsorrel, it's not a Woodsorrel Mite. Remember: "Woodsorrel home, woodsorrel mite" as your identification rule.
contextualKnowledge: Note that "woodsorrel" plants are sometimes called "shamrock" or "sourgrass" by gardeners, but they're completely different from true shamrocks (clover species). The sour, lemony taste of woodsorrel leaves comes from oxalic acid, which may actually influence the mites' preference for these particular plants.
compareHints: Since there are no other Petrobia species commonly found in New England, compare Woodsorrel Mites to other spider mites by their host plant specificity – most spider mites are generalists that feed on many plant species, while Woodsorrel Mites are specialists found almost exclusively on Oxalis. Other spider mites also tend to be more variable in color and create denser webbing patterns.
